titulo.texto: Alameda Central: the Oldest Public Park in the Americas

frase_gancho.texto: It is called Alameda after some poplars that did not survive, and the viceroy ordered it built in fifteen ninety-two.

puente_narrativo.texto: Follow the pathways into the park. Among the trees the first fountains appear, and each one brings its own story.

como_llegar.texto: Leave the palace and cross over to the Alameda Central, the park that stretches out in front of the esplanade. Follow its pathways to the next stop.

guion_corto.texto: Alameda comes from álamo, the Spanish word for poplar, but the poplars did not stay. The first trees were replaced by ash trees and willows, and the name survived. In January of fifteen ninety-two, Viceroy Luis de Velasco asked the city council to build a park in front of the church of Santa Veracruz. It is considered the oldest public park in the Americas. It was a promenade for the townspeople, but also a place of contrasts, because beside its western edge stood the burning ground of the Inquisition. Over time it filled with fountains, sculptures, and street lamps. Today it is a space open to everyone and the hub of this first zone of the tour.

guion_largo.texto:
Imagine this place at the end of the sixteenth century. You are on the outskirts of the city, to the west. The area had been a market west of the ancient Tenochtitlan. In January of fifteen ninety-two, Viceroy Luis de Velasco asked the city council for a park next to the church of Santa Veracruz, for the recreation of the townspeople. It is the first public park of New Spain.

The original layout was square, and it was carried out by the master builder Cristóbal Carballo. Poplars were planted, but over time they were replaced by ash trees and willows. The name stayed in memory of those first trees.

Not everything was leisure. Beside the western side stood the burning ground of the Holy Inquisition, where people condemned for heresy were executed during the height of that tribunal. It is one of the reasons the Alameda has always been a place of contrasts.

In the second half of the eighteenth century, the park doubled in size by incorporating the side plazas, and it has been rectangular ever since. At that time, during the governments of the viceroys Bucareli and Revillagigedo, fountains with sculptures of mythological themes were installed. Later, in 1821, the Army of the Three Guarantees rested here.

The nineteenth century changed the landscape. The viceregal sculptures were replaced by new works, several of them made in France, which you will see at the next stop. First there were turpentine lamps, then gas burners, and in 1892 electric light arrived. In 1905 the Moorish Kiosk was installed in this garden, and today it stands in the Santa María la Ribera neighborhood. In its place, years later, the [Hemicycle to Juárez](cdmx_05_hemiciclo_juarez) was built.

The twentieth century also left its mark. In February of 1968, the Spanish singer Raphael gave a concert in this park. Between 1973 and 1983 the irrigation and drainage were replaced. The walkways were also paved and the fountains repaired. In those years several marble sculptures were replaced by replicas.

In 1947, Diego Rivera painted a mural that has this Alameda as its setting. It is called Sueño de una tarde dominical en la Alameda Central, which means “Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda Central,” and you will see it in [the Diego Rivera Mural Museum](cdmx_06_museo_mural_rivera).

The most recent major intervention was in 2012, as part of the management plan for the Historic Center. The damaged paving was replaced with marble and the gardens were replanted. Today the park is a place for passing through and resting, with fountains, benches, and sculptures, just steps from the [Palacio de Bellas Artes](cdmx_01_bellas_artes). It is also the backbone of this stretch of the tour.

As you walk along its pathways, think that you are crossing a park that has spent more than four centuries changing its shape, its trees, and its ornaments. Each generation left it something: a layout, a fountain, a street lamp, a bench. And yet it keeps the idea with which it was born, that of a place where the townspeople can stroll and meet.

texto: Look at the floor of the pathways: since the 2012 renovation it has been made of marble
Count the fountains with sculptures that you find along the way
Look for the Hemicycle to Juárez at the edge of the park that faces Juárez Avenue

texto.Era: founded by order of the viceroy in 1592
texto.Style: viceregal park transformed in the 18th and 19th centuries
texto.Location: Av. Juárez, between Eje Central and Dr. Mora
texto.Key fact: it is considered the oldest public park in the Americas

texto.pregunta: Myth: In 1846 the fountains of the Alameda were filled with aguardiente to celebrate Santa Anna’s triumph.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a legend told about the park, not a proven fact.
